transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Mr. Hassan, thank you for coming in to see me. I have some difficult news to share regarding your immunotherapy dose yesterday.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I can tell by your face. What now?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: There was a mistake. We gave you your dose on the wrong day of your cycle because of an error in our calendar entry. I am very sorry. I take full responsibility for this mistake.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: You're joking. Again?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I know this is a lot to take in.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: No, I mean, again. Every time I come here, something "unfortunate" happens. First it was the pharmacy, then the nurse, now the calendar. Is this just how this clinic runs?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I can see how frustrating this is. This is a failure on our part, and I apologize.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Frustrating isn't the word. I'm tired. I'm just exhausted with the incompetence. Does this mean the drug didn't work? Does it mean my cancer is growing while you guys are playing with calendars?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I hear you. It's an incredibly heavy burden to keep dealing with these errors when you're already fighting this illness. Regarding the effectiveness, because the dose was administered too early in the cycle, there is a possibility that the treatment will be less effective for this specific round.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: A possibility. So you don't actually know.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: That's correct. We can't know for sure until we see the next set of scans, but the timing is critical for the drug to work the way it's supposed to.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Great. Just great. I'm sitting here in chronic pain, barely sleeping, and I've got a doctor who can't read a calendar.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I realize how unfair this feels.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I don't want your "realizations." I want to know why this happened. Who actually messed up?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It was my error in the scheduling system. I entered the date incorrectly.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: And nobody checked it? Not one person?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: No, and that is a failure of our process. I am truly sorry.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I've heard "sorry" from this building about six times this year. It doesn't actually change the fact that my treatment is potentially compromised.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It doesn't. I know an apology doesn't fix the dose or the stress this puts on you.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: So what happens now? Do I just wait and hope for the best?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: We will have to monitor things closely.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: That's not a plan. That's a suggestion. Do I need another dose? Do I skip the next one? What is the actual move here?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: We'll likely just continue as planned, but I need to check with the attending.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Check with who? You're the one talking to me. Give me a date. Give me a step.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I'll send an email to the specialist.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: An email. Wonderful. And when do I hear back? Next week?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I'm not entirely sure on the turnaround time for the response.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: This is exactly what I'm talking about. You're sorry, you're "holding space" for my anger, but you have no clue how to fix the mess you made.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I understand why you're cynical about this.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I'm not cynical, I'm observant. What is the actual, concrete plan for my next dose?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I'll look into it and we will see.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: See what?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Just see what the options are.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I can't believe this. I am literally gambling with my life and you're telling me to "see what the options are."

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I know this is an incredibly stressful situation.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Stop saying that. Just tell me when you will call me with a real answer.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I'll try to get back to you soon.

H.justification: Resident allows the patient to finish turns and remains regulated under significant pushback, with no interruptions or rushing language.

E.justification: The error was named explicitly in the first turn, but there were no comprehension checks performed throughout the encounter.

A.justification: Resident used direct apology language, took full personal responsibility for the calendar error, and maintained accountability despite the patient's anger.

R.justification: Resident named specific emotions ('frustrating', 'heavy burden', 'unfair', 'cynical') and referenced the patient's specific struggle with illness and chronic pain.

T.justification: The resident provided only placeholders ('we'll see', 'look into it') and failed to provide a concrete timeline or specific next steps.
